---
title: "Running INTEGRATOR"
description: |
  The four INTEGRATOR processing steps: data validation, peak finding and RT-shift estimation,
  peak integration, and optional PDF generation.
---

![flow chart for MRMhub
INTEGRATOR](images/workflow.png){fig-align="center"}

Upon execution, the software launches a terminal user interface with
four menu options. For new datasets, steps 1 and 2 are applied
sequentially. The final step 4 is optional and used only when
integration results as PDF files are required.

![](images/MRMhub-Main.png){fig-align="center" width="622" fig-alt="Screenshot of the INTEGRATOR terminal interface, showing the MRMHUB banner and its four-item menu: 1 Validate data; 2 RT-shift estimation and feature detection; 3 update integration bounds and areas using RT_matrix.csv; and 4 generate chromatogram PDFs (optional)."}

## Step 1 — Data Validation

The first step verifies the files and information provided in the input
files. Inconsistencies are reported in text files saved to the same
directory as the **MRMhub** application. These files are generated only
when issues are identified.

-   **`missing_files.txt`** lists mzML files that are present in the
    data folder but not listed in the Sample List, as well as files
    listed in the Sample List but absent from the data folder.
-   **`missing_compounds.txt`** reports transitions defined in the
    Transition List but not found in all mzML files. *Note:* Transitions
    present only in a subset of the mzML files are currently not
    processed.
-   **`missing_details.txt`** details the missing transitions and
    identifies exactly which samples lack them. This is useful when a
    transition appears in some samples but not others.

## Step 2 — Peak Finding and RT-shift estimation

The second step runs the peak finding and picking algorithm (see
[Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm](algorithm.qmd) for how it works). The result
of this step is a table of identified peaks (features) with their left
and right peak borders in each sample. This table is saved as the CSV
file `RT_matrix.csv` in the same folder as the application and is
required for step 3.

These integration bounds may be refined further on a per-transition and
per-sample basis before peak integration is performed in step 3. For a
new dataset, the recommended approach is to proceed directly to peak
integration, followed by visualization of the results in steps 3 (and
4), and to adjust specific integration borders manually only afterward.
Manual adjustment is generally discouraged unless certain integrations
can only be achieved through it.

At this point, the integration visualizer application **MRMhub-viz**
(see [MRMhub-viz Visualizer](viz.qmd)) can be launched to inspect the integration
results. Global and per-feature integration parameters can then be
revised (via param.txt and the Transition List), and peak integration
re-attempted via steps 1 and 2.

Once automated integration is considered optimal, final manual
adjustments to individual peaks can be made in `RT_matrix.csv` (see Step
2). After these optional manual adjustments, the final peak integration
is performed by (re-)running step 3.

**Warning**: Each time step 2 is executed, `RT_matrix.csv` is
**overwritten** and any manual modifications are lost.

## Step 3 — Peak Integration

In the third step, the peaks identified in step 2 are integrated and the
corresponding results saved to the following default output files:

-   **`quant_raw.csv`** A wide-format table of peak areas. The top three
    rows additionally contain the precursor and product m/z and peak
    apex retention time values.
-   **`long.csv`** A long-format table containing peak area, height,
    peak apex retention time, FWHM (Full Width at Half Maximum) and
    integration borders. The corresponding precursor and product m/z
    values, the analysis time stamp (extracted from the mzML files) and
    the metadata from the input files (sample type, ISTD, batch
    identifier) are also included.
-   **`misc`** A folder containing the peak integration results in a
    binary format, used by the visualizer application MRMhub-viz and in
    step 4.

All output tables are plain comma-separated CSV files. `long.csv` is the canonical hand-off to QUANT
(one row per *sample × feature*); `quant_raw.csv` is a wide-format export of peak
areas and is **not** read by the QUANT module.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## `long.csv` columns

These are the columns QUANT's `import_data_mrmhub()` reads from `long.csv`. Only `feature_name`
and `raw_data_filename` are strictly required (plus at least one intensity column); the rest are
metadata and measurements carried through to the `MRMhubExperiment`.

| `long.csv` column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `raw_data_filename` | Source mzML file name (becomes the analysis identifier) |
| `time_stamp` | Acquisition timestamp, read from the mzML |
| `sample_type` | Sample / QC type, from `run_order.csv` |
| `batch` | Batch identifier, from `run_order.csv` |
| `feature_name` | Feature (analyte) identifier, from the transition list |
| `internal_standard` | Assigned ISTD feature, from the transition list |
| `rt_apex` | Retention time at the peak apex (min) |
| `area` | Integrated peak area |
| `height` | Peak height |
| `FWHM` | Full width at half maximum |
| `rt_int_start` / `rt_int_end` | Left / right integration borders (min) |
| `polarity` | Ionisation polarity |
| `precursor_mz` / `product_mz` | Transition *m/z* values |
| `collision_energy` | Collision energy |

`quant_raw.csv` is a wide table of peak areas (features × samples); its top rows additionally
carry the precursor and product *m/z* and the apex retention time per transition.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
**Continue post-processing in QUANT.** The `long.csv` file is the canonical hand-off into the
QUANT R package: `import_data_mrmhub(path = "path/to/long.csv", import_metadata = TRUE)` loads the file
and its embedded metadata into an `MRMhubExperiment` for ISTD normalisation, drift/batch
correction, QC, and reporting. See the
[QUANT documentation ↗](https://slinghub.github.io/MRMhub/quant/).
:::

## Step 4 — Generate PDF results (optional)

The fourth step, which is optional, produces integration results as PDF
files. It creates three folders with different types of results:

-   `by_transition`: Contains one PDF per transition, with chromatograms
    plotted for each sample. Only transitions with at least one feature
    (peak) exceeding the *minimum intensity* threshold value are
    included here (see `by_transition_low`).
-   `by_transition_low`: Contains PDFs of transitions where none of the
    integrated features (peaks) had an area exceeding the *minimum
    intensity* threshold defined by the constant
    `low_intensity_threshold` in the provided `MRMhub_plot.r` R script.
-   `by_sample`: Provides a PDF for each reference sample; all of the
    sample’s transitions are plotted within the same file.

For efficient viewing of PDFs on macOS, open the PDF folder, press
*Space* to start Quick Look, then use the *up/down* arrow keys to move
between transitions (files). Use the scroll wheel or trackpad to
scroll through each PDF.

**Note**: In large-scale projects, generating many large PDF files can
take considerable time, depending on computer performance and the number
of cores used. The number of cores used to generate the PDFs can be
adjusted via the constant `ncores` in the provided `MRMhub_plot.r`
script.

::: {.callout-note}
**Reviewing retention-time stability at scale.** The per-transition PDFs provide an efficient means
of confirming that RT-shift correction has tracked the peaks across the entire analytical sequence.
In a published 4,591-sample lipidomics analysis, for example, RT shifts remained below 0.04 min
across the whole run, with the exception of approximately 20 samples at the start of one batch near
the end of the sequence, which were readily identified by scanning the `by_transition` PDFs. See the
[Dataset 3 workflow ↗](https://slinghub.github.io/mrmhub-workflows/Dataset3.html).
:::
